The microstructure and mechanical property of directionally solidified Ni–30.95Al–32Cr–6Mo–0.05Hf (at%)–0.1Dy (wt%) alloy were investigated
The master alloy of Ni–30.95Al–32Cr–6Mo–0.05Hf (at%)–0.1Dy (wt%) alloy (NiAl–Cr(Mo)–(Hf,Dy) for short) was prepared by vacuum induction melting.
The ∅ 7 mm rods were cut from the homogenized cast ingot by electro-discharge machining (EDM).
The temperature gradient at the solid–liquid interface was about 200 K/cm. The specimens were pulled down at the withdrawal rates of 6, 10, 30, 60 and 120 μm/s.
The microstructure consists of black NiAl and gray white Cr(Mo) lamellas from the observation of optical microscope.

It can be seen from Fig. 1 (a and b) that the solid–liquid interface is planar at 6 and 10 mm/s.
The solidification structure changes from planar eutectic to cellular eutectic with increasing the withdrawal rate to 30 mm/s, as shown in Fig. 1(c).

evidence.quote: When the withdrawal rate increases further, the solid–liquid interface morphology becomes dendritic, as displayed in Fig. 1 (d and e).

evidence.quote: The mean eutectic interlamellar spacing decreases with the increasing withdrawal rate, it decreases from 2.32 μm at 6 mm/s to 0.62 μm at 120 mm/s
Correspondingly, the area of intercellular region increases with the increasing withdrawal rate.
It is obvious that the mechanism of crack bridging occurs frequently during crack propagation due to the existence of Cr(Mo) phase.

The interface debonding occurs frequently at the intercellular region, as shown in Fig. 6 (a), which induced the crack deflection to the loading direction, thus resulting in an effective increase of fracture toughness.
the linkage of these microcracks with the main crack may provide further resistance to crack propagation.
a part of toughness may be attributed to the intrinsic toughening of NiAl phase by the generation of a high density of mobile dislocations.
